::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## What you will do

Fit gradient-boosted trees with XGBoost through the same workflow, watch the learning rate and the number of trees
trade off with early stopping, see that XGBoost can skip imputation, and then run the **bake-off**: logistic
regression, random forest, SVM and XGBoost on the same five folds, in one object, ranked with error bars.

**Time:** 30 min live coding + 15 min *Your turn*.
:::

## 0 · Start

```{r}
#| label: setup
# WHERE WE ARE ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# T1 pipeline + baseline (R/prep_nhms.R), T2 random forest, T3 SVM - all scored on the same folds with the same
# metrics, so they are comparable. NEW TODAY: the third family, gradient boosting with XGBoost, and then the
# BAKE-OFF: logistic vs RF vs SVM vs XGBoost in one workflow_set() on dm_folds, saved to outputs/ for later.
source("R/prep_nhms.R")
library(future)
plan(multisession, workers = max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 1))
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## 1 · Boosting in one paragraph

::: {.callout-note}
A random forest grows deep trees **in parallel** and averages them. Boosting grows shallow trees **in sequence**,
each one fitted to what the ensemble so far gets **wrong**. Start with a trivial prediction (the log-odds of the
prevalence). Compute, for every person, how wrong and in which direction — for classification that is the
**gradient** of the log-loss, which for each person is simply *observed − predicted probability*. Fit a small tree
to those residuals. Add it to the ensemble, shrunk by a **learning rate**. Repeat for hundreds of rounds. Each new
tree is a step downhill on the loss function — *gradient descent in the space of trees* — which is the same idea
that trains neural networks this afternoon. **XGBoost** is gradient boosting with serious engineering: a
regularised objective (λ on leaf weights, γ to prune splits that do not pay for themselves), split finding on
quantile sketches, a learned default direction for missing values, row and column subsampling, and multithreading.
:::

| `boost_tree()` | xgboost | Meaning | Start here |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trees` | nrounds | boosting rounds | 500 with early stopping, or tune |
| `learn_rate` | eta | step size | 0.01–0.1 |
| `tree_depth` | max_depth | depth of each weak learner | 3–6 |
| `min_n` | min_child_weight | minimum (weighted) people per leaf | 10–30 |
| `loss_reduction` | gamma | minimum gain to make a split | 0–1 |
| `sample_size` | subsample | row fraction per tree | 0.7–1 |
| `mtry` | colsample_bynode | columns per split (`counts = FALSE` → a proportion) | 0.5–1 |

XGBoost needs **numeric** predictors, so the recipe must dummy-code the factors (`dm_rec` does). Scaling is
irrelevant to trees but harmless, so one recipe serves all four families.

## 2 · "Just use the defaults" vs a gentle setting

```{r}
#| label: default-vs-gentle
xgb_default <- boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.3, tree_depth = 6) |>      # xgboost's own defaults
  set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")

xgb_gentle <- boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.03, tree_depth = 3, min_n = 20,
                         sample_size = 0.8, mtry = 0.7, loss_reduction = 1) |>
  set_engine("xgboost", counts = FALSE) |> set_mode("classification")

set.seed(2026)
xgb_two <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec), models = list(default = xgb_default, gentle = xgb_gentle)) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026)

collect_metrics(xgb_two) |> filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)
```

Same algorithm, same data, a visible AUC gap — purely from the settings. Boosting is **far** more sensitive to its
hyperparameters than a forest. "Which setting is best?" is an empirical question; Tutorial 5 lets the computer
search instead of guessing.

## 3 · Learning rate and number of trees trade off: early stopping

Hold out 20 % of each training set as a validation slice, let XGBoost watch the validation log-loss after every
tree, and stop when it has not improved for 25 rounds.

```{r}
#| label: early-stopping
fit_with_stop <- function(lr) {
  spec <- boost_tree(trees = 2000, learn_rate = lr, tree_depth = 3, min_n = 20, stop_iter = 25) |>
    set_engine("xgboost", validation = 0.2) |>
    set_mode("classification")
  set.seed(2026)
  workflow(dm_rec, spec) |> fit(dm_train) |> extract_fit_engine()
}

# the evaluation log lives in different places in xgboost 1.x and >= 2.x; this reads both
eval_log <- function(booster) {
  log <- attributes(booster)$evaluation_log
  if (is.null(log)) log <- tryCatch(booster$evaluation_log, error = function(e) NULL)
  as_tibble(log)
}

curves <- purrr::map_dfr(c(0.3, 0.05, 0.01), \(lr) fit_with_stop(lr) |> eval_log() |> mutate(learn_rate = lr))

curves |>
  ggplot(aes(iter, validation_logloss, colour = factor(learn_rate))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "number of trees", y = "validation log-loss", colour = "learn_rate",
       title = "Early stopping: where each learning rate stops improving") +
  theme_minimal()

curves |> group_by(learn_rate) |> summarise(best_iter = iter[which.min(validation_logloss)], best_logloss = min(validation_logloss))
```

A high learning rate reaches its minimum in a few dozen trees and then overfits; a small one takes hundreds of
trees to get there and ends lower. **Rule:** fix a learning rate in 0.01–0.1, then let early stopping or
cross-validation choose the number of trees — do not tune both freely.

## 4 · XGBoost handles missing values itself

Every split learns a *default direction* for rows where the splitting variable is `NA`. So XGBoost can take the
data **without imputation** — occasionally a better choice, because "missing" is then free to carry information
(people who skipped the weight question may differ from those who did not).

```{r}
#| label: native-na
rec_native_na <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>    # NA in a factor becomes NA in every dummy column - xgboost copes
  step_zv(all_predictors())

set.seed(2026)
xgb_na <- workflow_set(preproc = list(imputed = dm_rec, native_na = rec_native_na), models = list(xgb = xgb_gentle)) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026)
collect_metrics(xgb_na) |> filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)
```

Within noise here (7 % MAR missingness). Keep imputation when the same recipe must also serve a GLM, an SVM or a
network — they cannot cope with `NA`.

## 5 · The bake-off: four families, same folds, one object

```{r}
#| label: bakeoff
model_zoo <- list(
  logistic = logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm"),
  rf       = rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 6, min_n = 10) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification"),
  svm_rbf  = svm_rbf(cost = 1, rbf_sigma = 0.005) |> set_engine("kernlab") |> set_mode("classification"),
  xgb      = xgb_gentle
)

bakeoff <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec), models = model_zoo)
bakeoff

set.seed(2026)
bakeoff_res <- bakeoff |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026, verbose = TRUE,
               control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE))

rank_results(bakeoff_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc", select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "pr_auc", "brier_class")) |>
  select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err, rank)

autoplot(bakeoff_res, metric = c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) + theme_minimal()
```

This plot is the honest answer to "which model should I use?" — and the honest answer on this data is "three of
them are within one standard error of each other". When that happens, choose on everything *except* AUC:

| Criterion | Logistic | Random forest | XGBoost | SVM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Discrimination (tabular) | good | very good | **best, tuned** | good |
| Calibration out of the box | **good** | fair (shrinks to the middle) | fair | poor (Platt) |
| Interpretability | **coefficients** | importance | importance | none |
| Training / prediction speed | **instant** | fast / slower | fast / fast | slow (n²) / fast |
| Handles missing natively | no | no (ranger) | **yes** | no |
| Tuning sensitivity | low | **low** | high | high |
| Deployable as a paper score | **yes** | no | no | no |

One ROC curve per model, from the out-of-fold predictions:

```{r}
#| label: roc-all
collect_predictions(bakeoff_res) |>
  group_by(wflow_id) |>
  roc_curve(undx_dm, .pred_Yes) |>
  autoplot()
```

```{r}
#| label: save
saveRDS(bakeoff_res, "outputs/t04_bakeoff_res.rds")     # kept so you can reload it without re-running (nothing later requires it)
```

## Your turn (15 min)

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Task A · The five-minute XGBoost
Three settings of your own against `xgb_gentle`, on the folds (never on the test set). Think about learning rate × trees first.

```{r}
#| label: taskA
#| eval: false
boosters <- list(
  gentle  = xgb_gentle,
  model_1 = boost_tree(trees = ___, learn_rate = ___, tree_depth = ___, min_n = ___) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification"),
  model_2 = boost_tree(trees = ___, learn_rate = ___, tree_depth = ___, min_n = ___) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification"),
  model_3 = boost_tree(trees = ___, learn_rate = ___, tree_depth = ___, min_n = ___) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")
)
set.seed(2026)
boost_res <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec), models = boosters) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026, verbose = TRUE)
rank_results(boost_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc", select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)
```

**A1.** Did anyone beat `gentle` by more than one SE? **A2.** Did the deepest / fastest-learning setting win or lose?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution A

```{r}
#| label: solA
boosters <- list(
  gentle   = xgb_gentle,
  slow_deep = boost_tree(trees = 1000, learn_rate = 0.01, tree_depth = 6, min_n = 10) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification"),
  stumps    = boost_tree(trees = 1000, learn_rate = 0.05, tree_depth = 1, min_n = 20) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification"),
  fast      = boost_tree(trees = 200,  learn_rate = 0.3,  tree_depth = 3, min_n = 20) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")
)
set.seed(2026)
boost_res <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec), models = boosters) |>
  workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026)
rank_results(boost_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc", select_best = TRUE) |>
  filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)
```

`stumps` (depth-1 trees = an additive model) usually does surprisingly well — most of the signal is additive —
but loses a little to depth 2–3, which can express the family-history × BMI interaction. `fast` overfits. Slow and
deep is not better than gentle and costs four times the time.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Task B · Monotone constraints (stretch)
Biology says risk should never *decrease* with age in this range. Force it:
`set_engine("xgboost", monotone_constraints = ...)` needs a vector with one entry per predictor column
*after the recipe* (1 = increasing, 0 = free). Build it from `dm_rec |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL)`
column names, resample, and compare. (The warning about the sign being relative to the event level is expected —
read it.)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution B

```{r}
#| label: solB
pred_names <- dm_rec |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> select(-undx_dm) |> names()
mono <- as.integer(pred_names == "age")      # one entry per predictor column, in recipe order: +1 for age, 0 for the rest

# NB: splice the vector in with !!mono. Resampling runs on parallel workers, and they do not have `mono`
# in scope - set_engine() would otherwise just store the *name* `mono` and each worker fails with
# "object 'mono' not found". !!mono embeds the actual integer vector in the spec.
xgb_mono <- boost_tree(trees = 500, learn_rate = 0.03, tree_depth = 3, min_n = 20) |>
  set_engine("xgboost", monotone_constraints = !!mono) |> set_mode("classification")

set.seed(2026)
mono_res <- fit_resamples(workflow(dm_rec, xgb_mono), dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics)
collect_metrics(mono_res) |> filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class"))
```

Performance is essentially unchanged (the data already obey the constraint except at the very oldest ages, where
the simulated risk falls slightly — survivorship), but the model is now *guaranteed* to behave sensibly on
extrapolation, which is worth a lot when a clinician looks at a partial-dependence plot.
:::

## What to remember

1. Boosting = sequential error-correction; XGBoost = boosting plus regularisation and engineering.
2. Learning rate and number of trees trade off; fix one, let early stopping or CV choose the other.
3. Much more sensitive to settings than a forest — the reason Tutorial 5 exists.
4. `workflow_set()` + `workflow_map()` is how you compare families without copy-paste and without cheating.
5. When models tie within one SE, choose on calibration, interpretability, speed and deployability.

**Next:** Tutorial 5 — resampling and tuning (Session 6, 10.50).
